lines.text: The Memorial Student Center is the busiest building at Texas A&M.
So where can you actually study in peace, right now? Nobody had measured it. So we did.
On Saturday, we walked the first floor of the MSC in two rounds: once in the afternoon, and again in the evening.
At every study spot, we recorded twenty seconds of sound with the NIOSH Sound Level Meter app, which saves the average level, L-A-eq, as a PDF report.
We read the bottles-saved counter on all four water fillers,
photographed every vending machine and typed up its products, and checked the microwaves and printers.
That is a small dataset, but every number in it is real: twenty-five places on the map, nineteen noise readings, seven counter reads, thirty-six vending products.
Each value links back to its source, a PDF report or a photo. Nothing is simulated.
The quietest reading was the Flag Room's bottom-right corner, at forty-three and a half decibels.
The loudest was the Aggie Stop study spot: seventy decibels on Saturday afternoon. By the evening, the same spot had dropped to forty-seven.
Every ten decibels sounds about twice as loud. So when you go matters as much as where.
And the water fillers? Three of them filled just eight bottles in four hours. A quiet Saturday.
We turned it all into the MSC Study Guide: everything you need to study, on one map. Every study spot shows its noise level, next to the nearest water, restrooms and food, on a 3D plan of the floor.
Switch rounds to watch the floor change. Click a spot to see every measurement and its source.
Or open a vending machine in 3D and check what it sells.
Aggie Map tells you where things are. We tell you which one to pick, right now.
